g.text: From MapReduce to streaming — what an ending was answering
batch: 4 windows all final at event 9 · arrival-time pipeline: 3 of 4 wrong by 26
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · total 45 · 4 windows
A BATCH JOB OVER THIS DATASET
correct, scalable, fault-tolerant — and it requires the input to stop
what it reads
all 9 events, to the end of the input
what it computes
4 windows: 19, 11, 7, 8 · total 45
when each result is final
at end of input — event 9 — all of them at once
what it never needed
a watermark, a trigger, or an accumulation mode
Three of the Beam model's four questions are answered by accident here: WHERE is the input file, WHEN is end of input, HOW has no panes to
relate.
Remove the ending and all three defaults stop existing at once. That is the whole difficulty, and it is not about latency.
Step 1/4 — MapReduce made batch tractable, and assumed an ending
Start from what batch actually gives you: 4 window results, all final at event 9, with no watermark and no triggers needed. It is not that batch
lacks these mechanisms — it is that the end of the input answers three of the four questions for free. Take the ending away and all three answers
disappear together.
From MapReduce to streaming — what an ending was answering
batch: 4 windows all final at event 9 · arrival-time pipeline: 3 of 4 wrong by 26
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · total 45 · 4 windows
A PROCESSING-TIME PIPELINE, WHICH IS WHAT EARLY SYSTEMS OFFERED
low latency, no event time, no watermarks
batch (event time): 19 · arrival-time pipeline: 15
batch (event time): 11 · arrival-time pipeline: 2
batch (event time): 7 · arrival-time pipeline: 20
batch (event time): 8 · arrival-time pipeline: 8
3 of the 4 windows differ, by 26 in total. The pipeline is fast and answering a different question.
So the early trade was not "streaming is approximate" — it was "streaming had no way to express event time", which is a missing feature, not a
law.
Step 2/4 — early streaming got latency and lost correctness
Worth being precise about what early streaming systems lacked. They were not approximate by nature; they had no vocabulary for event time, so they
bucketed by arrival. That is 3 of 4 windows wrong here, by 26 in total — a missing feature rather than an inherent limit, which is why the model
could fix it.
From MapReduce to streaming — what an ending was answering
batch: 4 windows all final at event 9 · arrival-time pipeline: 3 of 4 wrong by 26
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · total 45 · 4 windows
THE SAME FOUR QUESTIONS, BOTH MODES
batch answers all four; it just answers three of them implicitly
WHAT
batch: the map/reduce · streaming: the aggregation — the SAME
WHERE
batch: the input file (one implicit window) · streaming: 4 explicit windows
WHEN
batch: end of input · streaming: when the watermark passes
HOW
batch: one pane, nothing to relate · streaming: accumulating or retracting
Read the WHAT row: it is identical. The computation was never the difference between batch and streaming.
The other three rows are all about TIME — which slice, which moment, and how successive answers relate. Those are the questions an ending used to
answer for you.
Step 3/4 — the four questions unified them
The unification is visible in the first row: WHAT is the same in both modes, and always was. The remaining three rows are all about time, and in
batch all three are answered by the input ending. So the model does not add machinery to batch — it names the three answers batch was getting for
free, so that a pipeline without an ending can supply them explicitly.
From MapReduce to streaming — what an ending was answering
batch: 4 windows all final at event 9 · arrival-time pipeline: 3 of 4 wrong by 26
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · total 45 · 4 windows
THE SAME PIPELINE, BOUNDED AND UNBOUNDED INPUT
the computation is the same; the finality is not
grouping, bounded input
grouping, unbounded input
4 windows: 19, 11, 7, 8 — identical
what differs
only WHEN each result is final
concretely
batch: all 4 final at event 9 · streaming: 1 never final
Identical groupings, identical values. The only difference is the last row — and it is a real one, not a formality.
Window [12:08, 12:10) holds 8 and is final in batch, never final in streaming.
Step 4/4 — so one pipeline can run in both modes
The payoff is concrete: the same pipeline code produces the same 4 windows with the same values in both modes, so backfill and live serving are
one codebase. And the honest caveat is in the last row — window [12:08, 12:10)'s 8 is final under batch and never final under streaming.
